# Problem 2

### loading libraries
```{r message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
```



### creating data frame

```{r message = FALSE}

study_df =
  tibble(
    files = list.files("data"),
    path = str_c("data/", files)
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(path, read_csv)
  ) |> unnest(data) |> 
  mutate(
    files = str_replace(files, ".csv", ""),
    arm = str_sub(files, 1, 3),
    subject_id = str_sub(files, 5, 6),
    arm = recode_values(arm, "con" ~ "control", "exp" ~ "experimental")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |> 
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |> 
  select(arm, subject_id, week, observation)

```

### spaghetti plot

```{r}

study_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, group = subject_id, color = arm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path() +
  facet_grid(~arm) +
  labs(
    title = "Observations Over Time By Participant",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Arm"
  )

```

From the spaghetti plot, it appears that subjects in the control group have 
have relatively stable observation values over time, while the observed 
outcome measure in the experimental group increases approximately linearly
over time from week 1 to week 8. 

# Problem 3

### simulated data sets

```{r}

# simulation

sim_t_test = function(n = 30, mu, sigma = 5) {
  sim_data = tibble(
    x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  )
  
  sim_data |> 
    pull(x) |> 
    t.test(mu = 0) |> 
    broom::tidy() |> 
    select(estimate, p.value)
}

# loop for mu = 1,2,3,4,5,6

set.seed(1)

mu_values = 0:6
output = vector("list", 7)

for (i in 1:7) {
  
  sims = vector("list", 5000)
  
  for (j in 1:5000) {
    
    sims[[j]] = sim_t_test(mu = mu_values[i])
    
  }
  
  output[[i]] = bind_rows(sims) |> 
  mutate(mu = mu_values[i])
  
}

sim_results = bind_rows(output)
```


### plots

```{r}

sim_results |>
  group_by(mu) |> 
  summarize(power = mean(p.value < 0.05)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line()+
  labs(
    title = "Power of a one-sample t-test by true mu",
    x = "True mu",
    y = "Power"
  )
  

```

As the true mean gets further away from the null of 0, power increases, as a larger
effect size is easier to detect. As power approaches 1, around mu = 4, it plateaus.

```{r}

full_plot = sim_results |> 
  group_by(mu) |> 
  summarize(mean_estimate = mean(estimate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = mean_estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "All samples",
    x = "True value of mu",
    y = "Average estimate of mu"
  )

rejected_plot = sim_results |> 
  filter(p.value < 0.05) |> 
  group_by(mu) |> 
  summarize(mean_estimate = mean(estimate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = mean_estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Samples where null was rejected",
    x = "True value of mu",
    y = "Average estimate of mu"
  )

full_plot + rejected_plot

```

For smaller effect sizes (mu = 1-3) the average estimate among rejected tests 
overestimates the true mu because only samples with unusually large estimates 
will be reach significance. As mu increases, power approaches 1, and the  
estimates are nearly all rejected so the average converges to the true value of
mu.
